body.heading: Why worms come up
paragraphs: After rain, the ground is wet and soft. Earthworms come up to the top of the soil, and you can often see them on paths and grass.
Worms breathe through their skin, so they love damp places. A wet day is a perfect day for a worm to travel.

body.heading: Watch how they move
paragraphs: Crouch down quietly and watch one worm. It stretches long, then bunches up short. That is how it crawls, because worms have no legs at all.
See if you can spot the thicker band around its body. Grown-up worms have one. Count how many worms you can find in one small patch of ground.

body.heading: Worms are garden helpers
paragraphs: Worms eat old leaves and mix the soil as they tunnel. This helps plants grow strong. Gardeners are always happy to see worms.
When you finish watching, leave the worms in peace. They have important work to do under the ground.

takeaway: Earthworms come up after rain, and watching quietly shows you how they stretch and bunch to move.
materials: A magnifying glass if you have one
safetyNotes: Look with your eyes only — worms are delicate, so do not pick them up. Watch out for slippery paths.
screenFreeExtension: Draw a wiggly worm path on paper and trace along it with your finger.
